summary: Path steering is a mechanism to discover paths to producers of Information-Centric Networking content and steer later Interest messages along a discovered path. It is useful for multipath congestion control and for measurement and management. This experimental specification derives from an earlier published design.

plainLanguage.summary: This RFC gives content networks something IP networks do not have: the ability to ask for the same data to travel along the same route as last time. The route is written down on the way back, and the next request carries that note so every router follows it.

questions: how does path steering help congestion control
subtitle: Discovering the path a content request took, then asking for the next one to take the same path.

tldr.problem: In a content-centric network the forward and reverse paths are symmetric, but a consumer has no way to pin later requests to the path an earlier one took, which limits measurement and multi-path congestion control.
tldr.mechanism: Each forwarder adds its own 12-bit Nexthop Label to a path label as the content travels back, so the reply carries the whole path; the consumer then puts that path label in the next request and every forwarder uses it to pick its outgoing interface.
tldr.outcome: The reply also tells the consumer which hop failed when a path becomes stale, and the label can be made opaque to the consumer with hop-by-hop symmetric encryption.

facts.label: Long paths that fit in 36 bytes

today: RFC 9531 is an Experimental RFC and has not been obsoleted or updated. The document states that it is a product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group, and it lists the open questions that further experimentation with path steering should address, including how much more accurate measurements become and how much multi-path forwarding improves.

sections.title: Discovering and Reusing a Path
sections.content:
Path steering is a mechanism to discover paths to the producers of ICN Content Objects and steer subsequent Interest messages along a previously discovered path. It has various uses, including the operation of state-of-the-art multi-path congestion control algorithms and for network measurement and management. The specification derives directly from the design published in the referenced paper and does not recapitulate the design motivations, implementation details or evaluation of the scheme; that publication should be considered a normative reference, and where the technical details differ, the design documented here is definitive.

Path discovery and subsequent path steering in ICN networks are facilitated by the symmetry of forward and reverse paths in the Content-Centric Networking and Named Data Networking architectures. Path discovery is achieved by a consumer endpoint transmitting an ordinary Interest message and receiving a Content message containing an end-to-end path label constructed on the reverse path by the forwarding plane. Path steering is achieved by a consumer endpoint including a path label in the Interest message, which is forwarded to each nexthop through the corresponding egress interfaces in conjunction with Longest Name Prefix Match lookup in the Forwarding Information Base.

The document sets out use cases that justify extending ICN architectures with these capabilities. They include the discovery, monitoring and troubleshooting of multi-path network connectivity based on names and name prefixes, analogous to the traceroute and ping tools that have proven crucial in IP; the ICN Ping and ICN Traceroute specifications already exist for CCNx and are both capable of exploiting path steering if available. They also include accurate online measurement of network performance, which generally requires multiple consecutive packets to follow the same path under the control of an application; improving the performance and flexibility of multi-path congestion control algorithms, which depend on a consumer being able to steer packets onto individual paths; and allowing a consumer to mitigate content poisoning attacks by directing its Interests onto network paths that bypass poisoned caches.

One nuance compared to other path-aware networking approaches is that ICN path steering piggybacks path discovery on the base ICN data exchange rather than having a separate path advertisement or discovery mechanism. When the recorded path comes back in a Data message, the properties of the path are known only implicitly to the consumer rather than being explicitly labelled, which makes the choice of a path a question of observation or measurement rather than advance selection based on an advertised property.

The document is a product of the IRTF Information-Centric Networking Research Group and has received detailed review by experts in both the CCNx and NDN communities.
sections.plainLanguage: This RFC gives content networks something IP networks do not have: the ability to ask for the same data to travel along the same route as last time. The route is written down on the way back, and the next request carries that note so every router follows it.

sections.title: Path Discovery, Path Steering and Path Labels
sections.content:
Path Discovery is the process of sending an Interest message requesting discovery of a path and, if successful, receiving a Data message containing a path label for the path the corresponding Interest traversed.

Path Steering is the process of sending an Interest message containing the path label of a previously discovered path so that the forwarders use that path when forwarding that particular Interest message.

A Path Label is an optional field in the packet indicating a particular path from a consumer to either a producer or a forwarder cache that can respond with the requested item. In an Interest message, the path label gets built up hop by hop as the Interest traverses a path. In a Data message, the path label carries the full path information back to the consumer for use in one or more subsequent Interest messages.

A Nexthop Label is one entry in a path label representing the next hop for the corresponding forwarder to use when a path-steered Interest message arrives at that forwarder. A sequence of Nexthop Labels constitutes a full path label.
sections.plainLanguage: Three terms matter. Discovery is finding out which route your request took. Steering is telling the network to use that route next time. The route itself is written down as a path label, which is a list of Nexthop Labels, one per router.

sections.title: How Discovery and Steering Work
sections.content:
End-to-end path discovery for CCNx is achieved by creating a path label and placing it as a hop-by-hop TLV in a CCNx Content message. The path label is constructed hop by hop as the message traverses the reverse path of transit forwarders. The path label is updated by adding the Nexthop Label of the interface at which the Content message has arrived to the existing path label. Eventually, when the Content message arrives at the consumer, the path label identifies the complete path the Content message took to reach the consumer.

When multiple paths are available, subsequent Interests may be able to discover additional paths by omitting a path steering TLV and obtaining a new path label on the returning Interest.

Due to the symmetry of forward and reverse paths, a consumer application can reuse a discovered path label to fetch the same or a similar Content message, such as the next chunk or the next pointer in a Manifest, over the discovered network path. This path steering is achieved by processing the Interest message's path label at each transit forwarder and forwarding the Interest through the specified nexthop among those identified as feasible by Longest Name Prefix Match lookup in the Forwarding Information Base.

At a forwarder, an Interest arrives at the Content Store and then the Pending Interest Table. If the Interest carries no path label, the forwarder aggregates as usual and looks up the route. If it carries a path label, the forwarder reads the Nexthop Label and selects the egress interface from the FIB entry that the label lookup produced, matching the label against the nexthops of that FIB entry. If the label does not match any of them, the label is invalid. If the FIB has no route at all, the forwarder returns an InterestReturn with a no-route code.
sections.plainLanguage: The content comes back along the route it went out on, and each router on the way back adds its own interface number to a list. When the consumer receives it, the list is the complete route. The consumer then puts that list in the next request, and each router reads its own entry from the list and uses the matching outgoing interface.

sections.title: The Path Label Encoding
sections.content:
The specification chooses the polynomial encoding for representing a path label, which achieves reasonable space efficiency at the cost of establishing a hard limit on the length of paths that can be represented. The polynomial encoding uses a fixed-size bit array, and each transit forwarder is allocated a fixed-size portion of it. This design allocates 12 bits, that is 4095 as a generator polynomial, to each intermediate forwarder. This matches the scalability of today's commercial routers, which support up to 4096 physical and logical interfaces and usually do not have more than a few hundred active ones.

A forwarder that receives a Content message encodes the Nexthop Label in the next available slot and increments the label index. A forwarder that receives an Interest message reads the current Nexthop Label and decrements the label index. The extra computation required at each hop is therefore minimal compared with FIB lookup and other required operations. The result is that individual path label TLV instances are of a fixed pre-computed size, which places a hard upper bound on the maximum number of network hops that can be represented. This is not a significant practical problem in NDN and CCNx, since the size can be preset during Content message encoding based on the exact number of network hops the Interest traversed. Even long paths of 24 hops fit in a path label bitmap of 36 bytes with a 12-bit Nexthop Label.

A path label TLV is the tuple of flags, Path Label Hop Count, Nexthop Label and the path label bitmap. Three flags are assigned: DISCOVERY_MODE 0x00, FALLBACK_MODE 0x01 and STRICT_MODE 0x02, with 0x03 to 0xFF unassigned.

The Path Label Hop Count MUST be incremented by forwarders if the Interest packet carries a path label and the DISCOVERY_MODE flag is set. A producer node or a forwarder with a cached Data packet MUST use the Path Label Hop Count in calculating a bitmap size suitable for encoding the entire path to the consumer, and the count MUST be set to zero in newly created Data or InterestReturn packets. A consumer node MUST reuse the Path Label Hop Count together with the bitmap in order to correctly forward later Interests along the corresponding network path.

For CCNx, the path label is an optional hop-by-hop header TLV that can appear in Interest, InterestReturn and Content Object packets, with a 16-bit type, a 16-bit length, an 8-bit flags field, an 8-bit hop count, a 16-bit Nexthop Label and the bitmap. For NDN, the path label is an optional TLV for Interest and Data packets carried in the NDN Link Adaptation Protocol, chosen over the NDN packet itself because it can carry hop-by-hop information that mutates at each hop and therefore cannot be part of the secured hash or signature. It can also be used instead of the existing NextHopFaceId TLV, since it manages the selection and forwarding over an entire path rather than a single outgoing face.

For IANA, the value 0x000A has been assigned to T_PATH_LABEL in the CCNx Hop-by-Hop Types registry, and the value 0x0A to T_RETURN_INVALID_PATH_LABEL in the CCNx Interest Return Code Types registry. Five TLV type numbers are suggested for NDN: 0x0A for the path label itself, 0x0B for the flags, 0x0D for the bitmap, 0x0E for the Nexthop Label and 0x0F for the hop count.
sections.plainLanguage: The route is stored as a fixed-size table of small numbers, one per hop, with an index saying how far along the route you are. Twelve bits per hop is enough for any router's interface count. Because the size is fixed, the router only has to read one entry and move on, which keeps the extra work at each hop small.

sections.title: Handling Path Steering Errors
sections.content:
Over time, the state of interfaces and the FIB on forwarders may change such that, at any particular forwarder, a given nexthop is no longer valid for a given prefix. The path label will then point to a now-invalid nexthop. This is detected by failure to find a match between the decoded nexthop identifier and the nexthops of the FIB entry after the Longest Name Prefix Match lookup.

On detecting an invalid path label, the forwarder SHOULD respond to the Interest with an InterestReturn. The document therefore defines a new invalid path label response code for the InterestReturn message and includes the current path label as a hop-by-hop header. Each transit forwarder processing the InterestReturn updates the path label in the same manner as for Content messages, so that the consumer receiving the InterestReturn can easily identify which path label is no longer valid.

A consumer may alternatively request that a forwarder detecting the inconsistency forward the Interest by means of normal FIB lookup rather than return an error. The consumer endpoint, if it cares, can keep enough information about outstanding Interests to determine whether the path label sent with the Interest fails to match the path label in the corresponding returned Content, and use that to replace stale path labels. It does so by setting the FALLBACK_MODE flag of the path label TLV in its Interest message. Forwarders MUST fall back to Longest Name Prefix Match lookup if an Interest packet carries an invalid Nexthop Label and the FALLBACK_MODE flag is set. With the STRICT_MODE flag set, forwarders MUST respond with an InterestReturn specifying the new T_RETURN_INVALID_PATH_LABEL code, and MUST respond with the existing T_RETURN_MALFORMED_INTEREST code if both the FALLBACK_MODE and STRICT_MODE flags are set.

There is also an interaction with Interest aggregation. If two or more Interests matching the same Pending Interest Table entry arrive at a forwarder, under current behaviour they will be aggregated whether or not they carry identical path label TLVs. If a DISCOVERY_MODE Interest arrives first, it is forwarded and may discover a new path while the other Interest is aggregated, so a path label carried by that other Interest may be ignored. If the two arrive in the reverse order, the DISCOVERY_MODE Interest is aggregated and the consumer does not achieve its desire to discover a new path. Multiple Interests intended to discover paths may also be aggregated, which limits the ability to discover multiple paths in parallel and instead requires incremental discovery. Hence, when employing path steering, it is RECOMMENDED that such applications craft their Interests with unique name suffixes in order to avoid being aggregated.
sections.plainLanguage: A recorded route goes stale when the network changes. The router notices that its own entry no longer names an interface it has, and by default sends back a complaint. The consumer can ask instead for the router to just pick the normal route, which is what the fallback flag does, and it can then notice the mismatch itself and use a fresh label next time.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A path is invalidated by renumbering one or more Nexthop Labels. A malicious consumer can attempt to mount an attack by transmitting Interests with path labels that differ only in a single now-invalid Nexthop Label, in order to brute-force a valid one. If such an attack succeeds, a malicious consumer would be capable of steering Interests over a network path that may not match the paths computed by the routing algorithm or learned adaptively by the forwarders.

When a label lookup fails, by default, an invalid path label InterestReturn is returned to the consumer, and it contains a path label identical to the one in the corresponding Interest. A malicious consumer can therefore analyse the message's Hop Count field to infer which specific Nexthop Label had failed. Three countermeasures are given. A larger Nexthop Label is harder to crack, but this specification uses labels with much less entropy than a 32-bit label, so depending on computational hardness is not workable. A forwarder can periodically update Nexthop Labels to limit the maximum lifetime of paths, and it is RECOMMENDED that forwarders update path labels at least every few minutes. A void Hop Count field in an invalid path label InterestReturn would not give out the information on which specific label had failed, and an attacker might need to brute-force all Nexthop Labels in all combinations, but some useful diagnostic capability is lost by obscuring the hop count, since the locus of routing churn becomes harder to pin down. A forwarder MAY choose to invalidate the hop count in addition to changing Nexthop Labels periodically.

Because ICN forwarders maintain per-face state and forwarding state for Interest messages, state inflation attacks are a general concern. The addition of path steering does not meaningfully increase susceptibility to such attacks: the labels identifying each forwarding face are state proportional to the number of faces, and the path steering header inflates the Interest message and hence the Pending Interest Table state, but not by an amount that is a concern.

ICN protocols can also be susceptible to cache poisoning attacks, where a colluding consumer and producer arrange for bogus content to populate forwarder caches. These are generally confined to on-path attacks, but it is theoretically possible to launch a similar attack without a cooperating producer, so that the caches of on-path routers become poisoned with content from off-path routers. Without any prior knowledge of the network topology, the complexity of this attack is in the ballpark of breadth-first-search and depth-first-search algorithms with the additional burden of transmitting 2^31 Interests to crack a Nexthop Label on each hop. A relatively short periodic update of Nexthop Labels, together with heuristics in the ICN forwarder to foil label scans, may mitigate this.

If the countermeasures are not sufficient, the path label can be made opaque to the consumer endpoint using hop-by-hop symmetric cryptography. This is viable because of the symmetry of forward and reverse paths, combined with path steering requiring only reads and writes of the topmost Nexthop Label. A path-steering-capable forwarder receiving a Content message encrypts the current path label with its own non-shared symmetric key before adding a new Nexthop Label, and forwards the message downstream with an unencrypted topmost label and the remaining content encrypted. A forwarder receiving an Interest performs the label lookup using the topmost label, decrypts the path label with its own key, and forwards the message upstream. This does not require any key negotiation among forwarders and is no more expensive than MACsec or IPsec, and it is quite possible that encrypting only on the border routers of the trusted domains may suffice.
sections.plainLanguage: Because the labels are only 12 bits, an attacker could try many of them to find one that steers the traffic somewhere unwanted. Routers are advised to renumber their labels every few minutes, so any guess takes too long to be worth trying. Where that is not enough, each router can encrypt all but the current entry of the label, so a consumer never sees the whole route.

fields.name: Index
fields.desc: Position of the next Nexthop Label in the bitmap. It is incremented on the way back and decremented on the way out.

fields.name: Nexthop Label 1
fields.desc: The next hop the first forwarder on the path should use.

fields.name: Nexthop Label 2
fields.desc: The next hop the second forwarder on the path should use.

items.label: DISCOVERY_MODE
items.desc: The consumer is asking for a path to be discovered; forwarders increment the Path Label Hop Count.

items.label: FALLBACK_MODE
items.desc: If the Nexthop Label does not match, fall back to an ordinary longest-prefix lookup.

items.label: STRICT_MODE
items.desc: If the Nexthop Label does not match, return an invalid path label InterestReturn.
